{"id": "35:28/q16", "question": "What does إِنَّمَا restrict, and why this word order?", "turns_on": "Which element is restricted and whether the restriction is absolute or contextual.", "positions": [{"id": "35:28/q16/p1", "position": "The delayed scholars are restricted as the true fearers; reversing the order would emphasize God as the sole object feared.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Kalbi describe object fronting. Jurjani's two striking examples show that restriction falls on the delayed constituent, not one before illa; he cites 33:39 for the other sense. Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursevi, Alusi and Ibn Ashur concur, with Alusi citing 9:18. Qushayri makes innama emphatic and restrictive; Alusi rejects denial of restriction and reads an implicit rebuke of ignorant unbelievers."}, {"id": "35:28/q16/p2", "position": "The restriction is contextual or relative: ignorant polytheists lack fear, while believers' degrees of fear vary.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya gives contextual examples from Antarah and divine oneness; Ibn Ashur notes believers of the time count as learned and non-scholars can follow scholars. Abu Hayyan records Zamakhshari's stricter view and Ibn Atiyya's qualification."}, {"id": "35:28/q16/p3", "position": "If scholars were fronted for focus, the sense would be that they fear none but God.", "reasons": "Jurjani rejects this as the actual point, though he finds a related sense in 33:39."}]}
{"id": "35:28/q17", "question": "What readings make God or the scholars the subject?", "turns_on": "The transmission and case endings, then the sense assigned to khashya.", "positions": [{"id": "35:28/q17/p1", "position": "The common reading makes God the accusative object and scholars the nominative subject.", "reasons": "Jishumi, Sam in, Abu Hayyan and Biqai record it; Thalabi calls it correct. Jishumi rejects the rival as nonstandard, possibly a hypothetical gloss. Ibn al-Jazari and al-Daraqutni reject Abu Hanifa's attribution to a fabricated collection. Suyuti discusses unreliable anomaly chains, the need for Arabic, script and transmission, mutawatir and mashhur classes, and standard reading books; Burhan notes anomalous parsing's difficulty. Nashr also catalogs an unrelated vowel-transition class."}, {"id": "35:28/q17/p2", "position": "A reported reverse-case reading makes God the subject and scholars the object, with khashya figuratively meaning honoring, revering or knowing.", "reasons": "Attributed to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Abu Hanifa, Abu Haywa and Ibn Sirin; Sam in compares 2:124. Zamakhshari likens it to revering an imposing man, Razi to magnification, Burhan defends figurative awe. Biqai invokes mutual honor; al-Qayati cites a powerless but revered beloved. Jishumi and Thalabi also transmit 'knows.' Abu Hayyan doubts its attribution; Alusi records an independent Abu Haywa citation."}, {"id": "35:28/q17/p3", "position": "In the reverse-case reading, khashya can mean choosing: God selects the scholars.", "reasons": "Ibn Umar gives this explanation; Alusi cites a poem whose khashitu my cousins means selected, and Jishumi and Thalabi also mention it."}, {"id": "35:28/q17/p4", "position": "A passive reading yields that scholars revere God.", "reasons": "Nasafi attributes the passive form to Abu Hanifa, Ibn Abd al-Aziz and Ibn Sirin; this differs from reports of simple case reversal."}]}
{"id": "35:28/q18", "question": "Can إِنَّمَا be parsed differently?", "turns_on": "Whether ma is a relative pronoun or a blocking particle.", "positions": [{"id": "35:28/q18/p1", "position": "Ma may be relative, with scholars its predicate and an implicit referent in yakhsha.", "reasons": "Burhan notes ma can collectively denote rational persons and cites 4:3."}, {"id": "35:28/q18/p2", "position": "Ma can block a governing particle from acting.", "reasons": "Burhan describes this third type and elsewhere notes that some fronting is ordinary grammatical object-before-subject order."}]}
{"id": "35:28/q19", "question": "Was this verse revealed about a particular person?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:28/q19/p1", "position": "Reports say it was revealed about Abu Bakr when his fear became visibly apparent.", "reasons": "Ata al-Khurasani's raised report adds the Prophet's conversation with him and the maxim that greater knowledge brings greater fear; Abu Hayyan and Alusi transmit the shorter account."}]}
{"id": "35:28/q20", "question": "How does knowledge rank beside worship and worldly pursuit?", "turns_on": "The rank of knowledge and the condition of acting on it.", "positions": [{"id": "35:28/q20/p1", "position": "Knowledge raises scholars above worshippers and worldly seekers because it produces piety and beneficial teaching.", "reasons": "Razi argues from 49:13 that honor tracks piety, then knowledge, though failure to act challenges one's claim. Mawardi calls God-fearers masters. Qurtubi cites a mursal report through Makhul; Durr reports the Prophet's comparisons and prayers by creatures for teachers; Study Quran summarizes Paradise, angelic prayers and prophetic inheritance. Ibn Masud contrasts insatiable seekers of knowledge and wealth by approval versus transgression (96:6–7); Elmalili calls knowledge the highest rank."}, {"id": "35:28/q20/p2", "position": "Knowledge must become worship and practice to benefit its possessor; worldly use of religion brings trial.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites Baydawi on following obligatory worship, and Elmalili links practice with 35:10. Kab warns of learning without action and seeking worldly gain; Abu al-Darda transmits a raised version without a grade. Bursevi's couplet warns that reading without doing leaves ignorance."}]}
{"id": "35:28/q21", "question": "Why does the verse end عَزِيزٌ غَفُورٌ?", "turns_on": "Whether forgiveness here is chiefly the paired theological motive or also a rhetorical completion.", "positions": [{"id": "35:28/q21/p1", "position": "Might calls for fear because God can punish; forgiveness gives pardon, repentance and hope.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Wahidi and Baghawi specify dominion and believers' sins; Razi pairs retribution and hope. Qurtubi adds reward; Baydawi contrasts persistent tyrants and repentant people. Biqai says nothing God wills is difficult and He erases sins; Alusi says pardon belongs to one capable of punishment. Elmalili warns against complacency; Tabatabai adds trust and longing. Ibn Ashur says divine independence need not discourage converts because repentance is accepted and scholars are promised forgiveness."}, {"id": "35:28/q21/p2", "position": "Ghafur is also a rhetorical completion after Aziz.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this view and a parallel verse by al-Ghanawi."}]}
{"id": "35:28/q22", "question": "How does the verse fit the surrounding passage and surah?", "turns_on": "The notes trace immediate links or a larger argumentative span.", "positions": [{"id": "35:28/q22/p1", "position": "Visible signs lead to knowledgeable fear, recalling 35:18 and leading into the Book and righteous action.", "reasons": "Nasafi notes the turn after 35:27; Baydawi says divine acts demonstrate power. Alusi, Bursevi, Elmalili and Tabatabai recall 35:18's receptive fearful people; Ibn Ashur links them to recitation in 35:29. Asad and Study Quran summarize creation, resurrection, revelation and oneness. Islahi reads 19–28 as contrasts between receptive living hearts and deprived ones, with 23–26 a parenthesis; rain nurtures growth as Quran nurtures good and exposes evil."}, {"id": "35:28/q22/p2", "position": "The broader discourse confronts opponents who demand prompt punishment instead of heeding the messenger.", "reasons": "Islahi says the demand harasses the Prophet and evades monotheistic warning; the messenger delivers truth and God decides when to punish. Rejection after warning brings destruction; Muhammad's universal mission includes People of the Book backing Quraysh. The following passage answers objections, and natural opposites serve a divine purpose."}]}
{"id": "35:28/q23", "question": "What related reports apply this verse's fear and mercy?", "turns_on": "The ancillary reports apply fear to mercy, recitation and learning.", "positions": [{"id": "35:28/q23/p1", "position": "The Prophet's tears for a dying child show divinely placed mercy and allow weeping without discontent.", "reasons": "Ibn Hibban gives Usama ibn Zayd's account of Zaynab's daughter; another version echoes the 'only ... from His servants' construction."}, {"id": "35:28/q23/p2", "position": "A Quran reciter's fear should sound in the voice and lead to reflection, humility and obedience.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir calls Jabir's connected chain weak because Abdullah ibn Jafar al-Madini and his teacher are weak; he disapproves entertaining musical modes. Hudhayfa's warning condemns song, chant and lament that fail to pass throats; another report includes appointing singers for performance over learning, with two further traits omitted."}, {"id": "35:28/q23/p3", "position": "Knowledge of divine greatness guards against vanity and deepens remembrance.", "reasons": "Alusi says knowledge can invite pride unless checked by greatness and cites Junayd on satisfaction following rooted recognition. Kuranyolu stresses nature study and a Muslim duty to pursue knowledge."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q01", "question": "Who are the disbelievers here?", "turns_on": "Ordinary disbelief or an inward state of distance.", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q01/p1", "position": "People who deny God, His oneness, His Book, or His messengers.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies denial of God's oneness; Bursawī includes denial of God's existence. Biqāʿī describes concealing rationally evident signs and arrogantly rejecting God's allies and callers. Islāḥī relates the warning to the Book's original deniers."}, {"id": "35:36/q01/p2", "position": "People veiled from the addressee, lacking any spiritual closeness or inheritance of the Book.", "reasons": "Qāshānī gives an inward reading: denial leaves them truly distant from

{"id": "35:36/q02", "question": "What does assigning Hellfire to them convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the lām denotes desert or exclusive and enduring assignment.", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q02/p1", "position": "Hell is the deserved recompense for their disbelief and deeds.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says they have no share of Paradise or its bliss; Bursawī calls disbelief the greatest sin and contrasts this fire with ordinary fire. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the lām marks desert and cites 2:24 and 3:131; he distinguishes the fire of sinful believers."}, {"id": "35:36/q02/p2", "position": "Hell is assigned exclusively and inseparably to them.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads the lām as exclusive assignment of their recompense."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q03", "question": "Why is لَهُمْ placed before the mention of Hell?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q03/p1", "position": "It creates anticipation, then lets the completed statement settle in listeners' minds.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies this effect of the fronted phrase."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q04", "question": "What is the fire in the inward reading?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q04/p1", "position": "It is the hell of nature, with unending deprivation and pain.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says its sufferers find neither death nor easing."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q05", "question": "What does the denial of death mean?", "turns_on": "Whether qaḍāʾ is a death decree, an act of destruction, or a figure for death's pains.", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q05/p1", "position": "No death is decreed for them, so they remain alive in torment without death's relief.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī says death never descends; Qatāda and Ibn ʿAbbās say dying would grant rest. Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Bursawī and Ālūsī specify no second death. Ālūsī favors a denied sentence over a redundant bare denial of dying. Ibn ʿĀshūr links the literal sense to their plea in 43:77. Qurtubī and Study Quran cite 20:74, 'neither die nor live'; Ibn Kathīr cites a sound Muslim report and 20:74, 43:74–77, 17:97 and 78:30. Biqāʿī contrasts ordinary fire, which finishes its victims. Rāzī says they wish for death but are denied it (43:77)."}, {"id": "35:36/q05/p2", "position": "They are not killed or destroyed, and therefore cannot find relief.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī offers this as an alternative needing no omitted word, citing Moses' killing in 28:15. Ibn al-Jawzī cites the same usage; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says they are not killed off."}, {"id": "35:36/q05/p3", "position": "Figuratively, they undergo the pains of death without its release.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says renewed skins keep them tasting torment, citing 4:56."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q06", "question": "How is فَيَمُوتُوا۟ read and construed?", "turns_on": "Whether the fāʾ introduces a subjunctive result or a coordinated indicative with retained nūn.", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q06/p1", "position": "The common reading drops nūn: the subjunctive follows negation through an implicit an and makes death its denied result.", "reasons": "Zajjāj, Abū Isḥāq, Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Bursawī and Ālūsī explain the implicit an. Abū Ḥayyān says this denies both sentence and resulting death, not affirmative arrival without dying. Burhān contrasts deletion and retention of nūn. Samīn rejects the alternative affirmative-result sense as impossible here."}, {"id": "35:36/q06/p2", "position": "The raised reading retains nūn and coordinates dying with the negated decree: neither happens.", "reasons": "Reported from al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā and al-Thaqafī. Thaʿlabī, Kashshāf, Qurtubī, Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn and Ālūsī compare 77:36. Al-Kisāʾī attributes its written nūn to verse-final position and says either construction works in either clause. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this reading weak; Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn report that judgment."}, {"id": "35:36/q06/p3", "position": "A hypothetical subjunctive construction affirms the first event while denying its sequel, but that sense is impossible here.", "reasons": "Samīn gives arrival without conversation as the analogous sense and rejects it for this verse."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q07", "question": "What is the force of qaḍāʾ here?", "turns_on": "A decree or the completed act of death.", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q07/p1", "position": "It is judging or decreeing, here a death sentence.", "reasons": "Jishumī links qaḍāʾ with ḥukm; Ibn ʿĀshūr allows literal judgment or God's decree."}, {"id": "35:36/q07/p2", "position": "It can mean causing death or completing a life.", "reasons": "Jishumī says it can mean finishing something completely or death as life's completion; Ibn ʿĀshūr allows causing death."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q08", "question": "How does the death clause relate to the preceding Hell statement?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q08/p1", "position": "It is an explicative substitute, spelling out their condition in Hell.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies the clause as an explicative badal."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q09", "question": "What does the sequence of withheld death and unrelieved torment stress?", "turns_on": "Absence of an ending and absence of adaptation or decrease.", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q09/p1", "position": "Their torment has neither an end nor a decrease.", "reasons": "Rāzī says death would be its strongest possible end, and the damned wish for it (43:77). He contrasts this lack of decrease with the blessed receiving an increase from God's bounty (35:30)."}, {"id": "35:36/q09/p2", "position": "Afterlife torment never becomes harmless through bodily familiarity.", "reasons": "Rāzī contrasts worldly pain: it neither kills them nor becomes so familiar that they cease to feel it."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q10", "question": "How is the passive لَا يُقْضَىٰ عَلَيْهِمْ parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q10/p1", "position": "عَلَيْهِمْ serves as the passive verb's deputy subject.", "reasons": "Samīn gives this analysis alongside the corresponding parse of ʿanhum after yukhafaf."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q11", "question": "What does the denial of lighter punishment cover?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause covers all mitigation or especially death as escape; changing flames need not ease pain.", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q11/p1", "position": "Their felt punishment is never relieved, reduced, or interrupted.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Bursawī say not even for an eye blink or instant. Jishumī distinguishes less amount, less severity, and interruption, finding reduction likeliest because eternity already implies continuity. Qurtubī invokes renewed skins in 4:56. Rāzī says agony remains severe at every moment. Study Quran says worldly respite and repeated chances to repent preceded final sentencing, citing 2:162, 3:88, 2:86, 16:85, 43:74–75."}, {"id": "35:36/q11/p2", "position": "The clause particularly denies relief through death, though flames may abate and intensify.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī reconciles it with 17:97: this kind of torment is not eased by death. Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguishes enduring punishment from temporary subsiding. Jishumī, Bursawī, Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī say renewed blazing prevents relief of pain; Yaḥyā links it with increase in 78:30."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q12", "question": "How is يُخَفَّفُ read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q12/p1", "position": "One transmission from Abū ʿAmr stills the fāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya through Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī name ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr. Samīn treats the separated form like a connected one and cites poetic أشرب; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also cites poetry."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q13", "question": "How are عَنْهُم and مِّنْ عَذَابِهَا parsed?", "turns_on": "Which phrase supplies the passive deputy subject, and whether min is additional.", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q13/p1", "position": "عَنْهُم is the deputy subject and مِّنْ عَذَابِهَا fills the other argument.", "reasons": "Samīn, Bursawī and Ālūsī present this analysis."}, {"id": "35:36/q13/p2", "position": "مِّنْ عَذَابِهَا is the deputy subject and عَنْهُم fills the other argument.", "reasons": "Samīn, Bursawī and Ālūsī give this alternative. Samīn attributes to al-Akhfash the possibility that min is extra; Abū al-Baqāʾ says if so its genitive object must be raised as deputy subject."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q14", "question": "What does the pronoun in عَذَابِهَا refer to and encompass?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q14/p1", "position": "It refers to Hell's punishment, including fire and reported intense cold.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr names zamharīr; Ālūsī says permanence of torment need not exclude cold or other forms."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q15", "question": "Can another person's greater punishment make one's own feel lighter?", "turns_on": "Whether comparison itself is excluded or each person's perception explains the lack of comfort.", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q15/p1", "position": "No; sufferers are wholly consumed by their own pain, so comparisons cannot relieve it.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports the qāḍī's rejection of comparative easing and explicitly prefers that view."}, {"id": "35:36/q15/p2", "position": "Each sufferer believes his own punishment exceeds the others'.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this alternative account of why another's suffering affords no comfort."}]}

{"id": "35:36/q19", "question": "Who is included in كُلَّ كَفُورٍۢ?", "turns_on": "Any unbeliever, an especially persistent denier, denial of blessings, or specifically a polytheist.", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q19/p1", "position": "Every disbeliever or denier of God and the truth.", "reasons": "Qatāda says everyone disbelieving in his Lord; Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil gloss every disbeliever. {"id": "35:36/q22", "question": "How does this warning connect with the preceding passage?", "turns_on": "The immediately preceding inheriting groups or the earlier promise to reciters.", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q22/p1", "position": "It turns from believers' reward to disbelievers' fate and confirms that all three inheriting groups enter Paradise.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī says Muḥammad's monotheist community has just been described. {"id": "35:36/q23", "question": "How do the condemned respond when they face punishment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q23/p1", "position": "They plead for another chance after ignoring worldly warnings, but their cries bring no relief.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu compares their futile plea with 23:107–108; Qurtubī says this passage proceeds to their speech."}]}

{"id": "35:36/q25", "question": "What does the nearby discussion of provision say about divine favor?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q25/p1", "position": "Wealth and children do not prove favor or unworthiness; provision tests gratitude or patience, and success appears in the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Islāḥī says the repeated opening has different force: verse 36 stresses God's control, so people should neither boast nor despair."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q26", "question": "Does ḍiʿf in the nearby discussion mean exactly double reward?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q26/p1", "position": "No; the Arabic word should not be restricted to a double reward.", "reasons": "Islāḥī explicitly rejects that restriction."}]}
{"id": "35:36/q27", "question": "Does perpetual negation require lan rather than lā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:36/q27/p1", "position": "No; lā can also express perpetual negation.", "reasons": "Burhān cites 2:255 and 7:40 to reject giving eternal force uniquely to lan."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q01", "question": "Whose warning is restricted by 'you only warn,' and in what sense?", "turns_on": "Whether 'only' restricts the act of warning, its benefit, a stage of the mission, the subject warned about, or God's foreknowledge of responders.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q01/p1", "position": "The restriction concerns effective warning: followers of the Reminder benefit and attain faith or salvation, while hardened opponents do not.", "reasons": "Yahya says recipients accept and heed; Tabari contrasts sealed polytheists and private neglect by hypocrites; Wahidi says warning the astray is as though they were unwarned; Kashshaf and Baydawi define its intended aim as faith; Ibn Atiyya and Kur'an Yolu deny restriction of the Prophet's audience; Tabrisi says all have already received warning. Biqai says the Prophet should not grieve over those God knows to be hardened (2:2); Qashani grounds responsiveness in luminous innate preparedness; Islahi calls for open hearts, reasoning beyond sense, and counsel."}, {"id": "36:11/q01/p2", "position": "The Prophet must warn everyone, since he cannot know in advance who will respond, though only responders benefit.", "reasons": "Razi says the command is general and its effect selective; he separately argues that the Prophet cannot know whom he will guide. Elmalılı says warning everyone protects those who respond even when most do not."}, {"id": "36:11/q01/p3", "position": "Warning began generally; after full delivery and stubborn mockery, only followers remained receptive.", "reasons": "Razi names mockery, turning away, and arrogance after complete delivery."}, {"id": "36:11/q01/p4", "position": "The warning addresses everyone about basic beliefs but followers specifically about practical duties.", "reasons": "Razi names prayer and almsgiving as duties for those already following; Samarrai says believers also receive reminders of their duties, citing the Prophet's kin and those fearing resurrection as audiences."}, {"id": "36:11/q01/p5", "position": "Those warned are existing believers, and warning alerts them to later lapses.", "reasons": "Alusi offers this to avoid treating warning already responsive believers as redundant."}, {"id": "36:11/q01/p6", "position": "The beneficiaries are those God knows will follow, the smaller group not subject to the decree.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this as another reading of the restriction."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q02", "question": "What is 'the Reminder' here?", "turns_on": "Whether dhikr designates the already mentioned Qur'an, admonition generally, or the signs and proofs by which one remembers God.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q02/p1", "position": "The Reminder is the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Yahya compares 35:18; Razi appeals to the definite article and the Wise Qur'an of 36:2; Study Quran compares 36:69. The Qur'an is followed through listening, recitation, reflection, affirmation, and practice in various sources; Kur'an Yolu calls this the majority view."}, {"id": "36:11/q02/p2", "position": "The Reminder is admonition or exhortation.", "reasons": "Kashshaf offers exhortation; Abu Hayyan attributes admonition to Qatada; Alusi treats it as an alternative and relates the past v

{"id": "36:11/q03", "question": "What does following the Reminder involve?", "turns_on": "Whether 'following' is described by outward response and practice or by the inward preparedness that makes response possible.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q03/p1", "position": "It involves receptive faith, reflection or listening, and acting on what is received.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Wahidi mention listening; Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and others stress action; Baydawi combines reflection and practice; Alusi does likewise; Elmalılı adds serious recitation and heeding admonition; Tabatabai says affirming and inclining as verses are recited; Razi calls following faith and connects it to forgiveness (35:28; 34:4); Asad notes the literal sense 'who is following.'"}, {"id": "36:11/q03/p2", "position": "It is the response of people whose pure, luminous innate readiness allows guidance and original knowledge.", "reasons": "Qashani connects receptivity to innate monotheism; Islahi says they open their hearts and reason with sight, hearing, mind, and heart before direct proof."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q04", "question": "Why is 'followed' in the past form?", "turns_on": "Whether the past marks certain future response or already completed adherence.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q04/p1", "position": "Its past form expresses certainty that following will occur.", "reasons": "Alusi applies this to the admonition reading; Tabatabai likewise says the occurrence is certain."}, {"id": "36:11/q04/p2", "position": "It describes believers who already followed, so later warning concerns future lapses.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this to avoid a redundant warning."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q05", "question": "Why is the one feared called 'the Merciful'?", "turns_on": "Whether the name chiefly balances hope against fear or shows how divine kindness alone moves the receptive.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q05/p1", "position": "The name joins fear with hope: mercy must not make one complacent, and punishment must not cause despair.", "reasons": "Razi contrasts divine names that evoke awe and affection and says withdrawing repeated gifts is fearful; Baydawi and Bursevi note divine vengeance or overpowering power despite mercy; Alusi cites 15:49-50; Elmalılı cites 15:49; Tabatabai says this balance sustains worship; Islahi says graciousness requires reward for piety and punishment for wrongdoing at the appointed Day."}, {"id": "36:11/q05/p2", "position": "Even reminders of God's kindness are enough to move the truly fearful.", "reasons": "Biqai sees a shift from majesty to mercy and describes their fear as intense."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q06", "question": "What is feared when one fears the Merciful?", "turns_on": "Whether fear is explained by punishment or by God's majesty and possible withdrawal of favor; several sources include both.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q06/p1", "position": "The person fears God's punishment, including the Fire, while holding hope in His mercy.", "reasons": "Qatada is reported by Ibn Abi Hatim, Mawardi, Qurtubi and Durr; Muqatil, Nasafi, Baydawi, Bursevi, Alusi and Elmalılı also speak of punishment. Alusi cites 15:49-50; Bursevi cites 70:28."}, {"id": "36:11/q06/p2", "position": "The person reveres God's majesty and fears losing His favor or blessings.", "reasons": "Razi says the withdrawal of repeated gifts would be grievous; Abu Hayyan mentions loss of blessings; Biqai includes lost favor and God's majesty; Bursevi says uninterrupted mercy makes its loss frightening."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q07", "question": "What does fearing 'in the unseen' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether al-ghayb concerns absence of human observers, the not-yet-visible divine realities or punishment, the hidden heart, concealed deeds, or mystical witnessing.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q07/p1", "position": "It means fearing or worshipping God privately, sincerely, when other people do not see.", "reasons": "Yahya stresses sincere inner faith; Zajjaj and Abu Ishaq say only God sees; Tabari and Jishumi contrast hypocrites, while Alusi contrasts ostentation. Ibn Kathir adds awareness that God sees and knows one's deeds; Biqai calls it fear without a human observer to impress; Study Quran compares 50:33. Ibn Jawzi points to 21:49 without restating the interpretation."}, {"id": "36:11/q07/p2", "position": "It means fearing God or His unseen punishment before death or resurrection makes realities visible.", "reasons": "Razi says evidence supports fear before sight, when fear still serves a purpose; Baydawi and Bursevi say punishment is feared before arrival; Alusi reports readings where the punishment or the fearing person is unseen; Tabatabai prefers fear behind the veil before death or resurrection to fear in human seclusion; Biqai rejects demanding a sign that removes the veil; Islahi calls faith before direct visual proof valuable."}, {"id": "36:11/q07/p3", "position": "It means fearing unseen matters of the afterlife, especially resurrection and the Fire, and perhaps divine unity.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabrisi report afterlife matters; Qatada's punishment and Fire belong to this reading; Razi calls resurrection realities common and reports divine unity as another included unseen matter; Biqai emphasizes unseen powers and resurrection."}, {"id": "36:11/q07/p4", "position": "It means inward fear in the hidden heart.", "reasons": "Alusi reports a grammatical construal making al-ghayb the heart, with the preposition attached to 'feared'; Elmalılı says only God knows this heart and distinguishes it from outward display."}, {"id": "36:11/q07/p5", "position": "It means concealing one's evil deeds from other people.", "reasons": "Mawardi reports this from al-Suddi."}, {"id": "36:11/q07/p6", "position": "It means inwardly witnessing the disastrous end of disbelief and the sweetness of faith.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this mystical interpretation from al-Ta'wilat al-Najmiyya, adding the rank of gnosis."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q08", "question": "What is the purpose and timing of 'give him good news'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q08/p1", "position": "Glad tidings follow beneficial warning as the second part of the Messenger's mission.", "reasons": "Razi calls it the second part of his task; Alusi reports Abu Hayyan that the conjunction orders good news after following and fearing, proving the warning benefited the person; Elmalılı says the mission's wisdom includes generous tidings as well as warning; Islahi says promise a great reward to those ready for counsel."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q09", "question": "Why is the recipient of good news singular?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q09/p1", "position": "The singular pronoun agrees with the singular form of 'whoever' and refers to the person who both follows and fears.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya explains agreement with man; Bursevi identifies the two qualifications; Biqai adds that the singular signals how few such people are in this comprehensive, heart-like surah."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q10", "question": "What does the promised forgiveness cover or signify?", "turns_on": "Whether forgiveness is explicated as pardon of sins or as inward removal of veils; both may be understood as vast.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q10/p1", "position": "It pardons the believer's sins, possibly including grave, repeated, past or future sins.", "reasons": "Yahya, Tabari, Zajjaj, Mawardi, Wahidi, Qurtubi and others specify sin; Biqai says grave and repeated sins do not cancel genuine fear when one repeatedly repents; Alusi reports past sins or possible future lapses; Razi and Elmalılı take indefinite form or nunation to magnify its extent; Ibn Kathir compares 67:12."}, {"id": "36:11/q10/p2", "position": "It is a vast spiritual veiling that removes the soul's traces or sins that veil divine realities.", "reasons": "Razi says the indefinite form implies forgiveness on every side, no trace of the lower self, and lights of the purified spirit; Qashani speaks of veils over God's acts, attributes, and Essence."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q11", "question": "What is the 'noble reward'?", "turns_on": "Whether ajr karim is identified by its destination, purity, abundance, honor, or an inward account of divine gardens; several descriptions can coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q11/p1", "position": "It is Paradise, with its beautiful, abundant, lasting and incomparable gifts.", "reasons": "Yahya calls it noble recompense; Ibn Atiyya adds praise and honor; Alusi reports Qatada that its greatest delight is seeing God; Bursevi calls its gifts incomparable; Biqai describes an immense pleasant continuous abode without discomfort; Tabatabai says indefinite wording makes it immeasurable; Ibn Kathir compares 67:12. Nahhas leaves the competing gloss to God."}, {"id": "36:11/q11/p2", "position": "Karim means a good or beautiful reward.", "reasons": "Nahhas reports Dahhak from Ibn Abbas; Jishumi and Tabrisi add that it is free of impurities."}, {"id": "36:11/q11/p3", "position": "It is an abundant or generous recompense.", "reasons": "Mawardi presents abundance as one interpretation; Razi calls the reward characterized by generosity and points to earlier explanations of noble provision; Ibn Kathir says great, abundant and beautiful; Elmalılı says it lacks deficiency."}, {"id": "36:11/q11/p4", "position": "It is a reward accompanied by praise and honor, given for obedience.", "reasons": "Mawardi presents honor as another interpretation and calls it the reward of obedience; Ibn Atiyya says the worker receives it with praise and honor; Elmalılı says it is without favor or deficiency."}, {"id": "36:11/q11/p5", "position": "It i

{"id": "36:11/q12", "question": "How do the two promised outcomes match following and fear?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q12/p1", "position": "Following or faith brings forgiveness, while fear and righteous deeds bring reward.", "reasons": "Razi explicitly pairs following with faith and forgiveness, and fear with works and reward, citing 35:28 and 34:4; Bursevi says reflection and admonition lead to faith and forgiveness, while fear leads to good deeds and reward, citing 56:24."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q13", "question": "Are denial and following the Reminder created by God or performed by people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q13/p1", "position": "They are human acts.", "reasons": "Jishumi rejects the Mujbira claim that God creates those acts."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q14", "question": "What inward conduct expresses sincere fear and worship?", "turns_on": "Tustari describes practical secret worship and fairness; Qashani describes an inward passage from veiling to presence.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q14/p1", "position": "Secret worship produces certainty; truthful speech raises the heart; fairness directs every limb to God and makes generosity toward people essential.", "reasons": "Tustari says fairness places heaven and earth in one's balance; concern over tomorrow's provision divides the heart's concern, while demanding fairness for oneself fails fairness."}, {"id": "36:11/q14/p2", "position": "The person remembers and fears God through His veiled majesty, then follows a path from absence to presence and sight.", "reasons": "Qashani describes the progression as seeing by the light of what was formerly absent."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q15", "question": "What is the highest station of those who remember God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q15/p1", "position": "They forget awareness of their own remembrance while witnessing the Remembered and guard their time from returning to self-awareness.", "reasons": "Sulami reports this from al-Husayn."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q16", "question": "What do the reports of John and Jesus illustrate about the heart's attention to God?", "turns_on": "The two reports emphasize different degrees of undivided heart attention.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q16/p1", "position": "John's body could be beside Jesus while his heart remained fixed at the Throne.", "reasons": "Tustari reports Sahl's account in which Jesus reproaches John after he struck a woman."}, {"id": "36:11/q16/p2", "position": "John said a moment of resting his heart in Gabriel would make him doubt that he truly knew God.", "reasons": "Tustari reports John's statement."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q17", "question": "How does this verse fit the preceding warning and the sura's opening?", "turns_on": "The sources connect the verse either to the immediately preceding failed warning, to the Abu Jahl episode, or to the sura's opening argument for prophethood.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q17/p1", "position": "It contrasts the unresponsive with those who benefit from warning, relieving the Prophet of grief over hardened hearers.", "reasons": "Kashshaf reconciles 36:10's failure of warning with its effective goal here; Alusi says the preceding opponents seemed unmoved; Study Quran compares 35:8; Islahi says leave nonlisteners to God, who records their deeds; Biqai cites 2:2 for the guided God-fearing."}, {"id": "36:11/q17/p2", "position": "The passage is connected with Abu Jahl and al-'Alaq's account of one who forbids a servant from prayer.", "reasons": "Muqatil connects it to 96:9-10."}, {"id": "36:11/q17/p3", "position": "Verses 1-12 establish Muhammad's prophethood through the wise Qur'an, God's favor to a people astray without guidance.", "reasons": "Islahi says arrogance, inherited traditions and future desires hinder reflection on the strongest proof of the messenger and his straight path."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q18", "question": "How does the following verse's resurrection imagery extend this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether revival in the linked discussion is literal resurrection or also the spiritual revival of hardened hearts.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q18/p1", "position": "God will raise the dead, and may also revive disbelievers' dead hearts through guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir compares 57:17; Bursevi reports al-Ta'wilat al-Najmiyya's shower of divine turning and closeness that revives hardened hearts."}, {"id": "36:11/q18/p2", "position": "The following verse speaks of literal revival with sensation and movement.", "reasons": "Bursevi defines revival this way, while noting the Prophet also called affluent people and unjust rulers dead."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q19", "question": "Who performs the revival mentioned in the following verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural divine pronoun permits angelic participation or emphasizes exclusive divine action.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q19/p1", "position": "God alone revives the dead; the plural 'We' expresses majesty and divine attributes.", "reasons": "Bursevi challenges the suggestion that angels share in revival because the emphatic pronoun denotes God alone; al-Bahr says the repeated pronoun adds emphasis and highlights recompense with honor or retribution."}, {"id": "36:11/q19/p2", "position": "Angels may share in reviving the dead.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this view only to challenge it with the emphatic 'We alone.'"}]}
{"id": "36:11/q20", "question": "What does the following verse mean by recording what people send ahead and their traces?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q20/p1", "position": "It records the good and evil deeds already done and lasting good legacies.", "reasons": "Bursevi lists teaching knowledge, writing books, endowing works, and building mosques, hospices or bridges; Sa'di's couplet says one does not die while a good legacy remains."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q21", "question": "Who writes people's deeds in the following verse, and why is writing mentioned after revival?", "turns_on": "Whether 'We write' refers directly to divine preservation or to recording angels acting by divine command.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q21/p1", "position": "God preserves and establishes the deeds in the Preserved Tablet.", "reasons": "Bursevi gives this as one sense of 'We write' and says writing follows revival in the wording because its purpose is resurrection."}, {"id": "36:11/q21/p2", "position": "Noble recording angels write at God's command, so the act is attributed to Him as warning.", "reasons": "Bursevi gives this alternative and likewise explains the order by writing's purpose in resurrection."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q22", "question": "What can 'dead' mean in the Prophet's adjacent report?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q22/p1", "position": "The dead can mean an affluent person or unjust ruler whose company kills the heart.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports a prophetic saying that repeated sin, excessive company and talk with women, arguing with a fool, and keeping company with the 'dead' are four heart-killing things."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q23", "question": "How is a mosque's neighbor defined in the adjacent excursus?", "turns_on": "Whether neighborhood is measured by distance in houses or audibility of the call.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q23/p1", "position": "Anyone within forty houses in each direction.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this from some authorities."}, {"id": "36:11/q23/p2", "position": "Anyone who hears the call to prayer.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this as another view."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q24", "question": "Which mosque should a worshipper choose when two are near?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q24/p1", "position": "Choose the older mosque, or if equal the nearer; a scholar may increase attendance at the smaller congregation.", "reasons": "Bursevi says the older mosque has greater sanctity and permits others to choose freely."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q25", "question": "What is the status and reward of congregational mosque prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the congregation's strongly commended status entails legal obligation or confirmed sunna; reported reward variants differ between twenty-five and twenty-seven.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q25/p1", "position": "Mosque congregation is preferable for obligatory prayers and tarawih and yields more reward than home congregation.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports a prophetic reward of twenty-five times that of praying at home or market; another wording says twenty-seven, matched to seventeen obligatory and ten regular prayers."}, {"id": "36:11/q25/p2", "position": "Congregational prayer is obligatory.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this as the view of most scholars; he cites the Prophet's contemplated order to burn absentees' houses as evidence for strong enforcement."}, {"id": "36:11/q25/p3", "position": "Congregational prayer is a confirmed sunna.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this from some scholars and argues that the house-burning report could concern abandonment of an obligation or a confirmed sunna; he says the Prophet would not intend a sinful act."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q26", "question": "What excuses permit missing mosque congregation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q26/p1", "position": "Illness, disabling injury, inability to walk, blindness, bad weather, severe darkness, or fear of oppression can excuse absence.", "reasons": "Bursevi specifies illness warranting tayammum, paralysis, rain, mud, cold, and fear of rulers or other oppressors; a report promises complete light on Judgment Day to those who walk to mosques in darkness, so he treats only severe darkness as an excuse."}]}
{"id": "36:11/q27", "question": "What purposes can repetition serve in Qur'anic speech?", "turns_on": "Whether discussing the purposes of repetition or its technical distinction from verbal emphasis.", "positions": [{"id": "36:11/q27/p1

", "position": "Repetition confirms, draws attention, removes suspicion, refreshes earlier points, or magnifies and overawes.", "reasons": "Itqan says repetition can be stronger than emphasis and cites 25:50 for remembrance; repeated 'O my people' at 40:38-39 raises attention; 16:119, 16:110, 2:89, 3:188 and Joseph's dream at 12:4 show refreshing; 69:1, 101:1 and 56:27 show magnification."}, {"id": "36:11/q27/p2", "position": "Repetition is a figure distinct from formal emphasis, especially when repeated wording is separated from its first occurrence.", "reasons": "Itqan says emphasis need not repeat wording, repetition may only emphasize meaning, and verbal emphasis cannot be separated from what it emphasizes; examples include 2:223 and 3:42."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q01", "question": "How is إنا نحن parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether نحن completes the predication or reinforces the subject of نحيي.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q01/p1", "position": "نحن is emphatic, and نحيي is the predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Razi prefers this analysis."}, {"id": "36:12/q01/p2", "position": "إنا نحن is a complete subject and predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Razi likens it to a famous person saying simply 'I': divine self-identification suffices because God is known by His attributes."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q02", "question": "Why the emphatic divine 'We'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q02/p1", "position": "It marks majesty, sole agency, and assurance of resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says God needs no name or lineage to distinguish Him and the wording signals oneness; al-Biqaʿi stresses protection of believers; al-Alusi says it answers resurrection deniers (45:24) and repeating نحن adds emphasis or exclusivity; Elmalılı gives majesty or 'We alone.'"}]}
{"id": "36:12/q03", "question": "What is the form of إنا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q03/p1", "position": "A nūn has been omitted from إننا to avoid three consecutive nūns.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas gives the phonological explanation."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q04", "question": "What does reviving the dead mean?", "turns_on": "Whether death is physical, figurative spiritual death, the earth's death, or an allusion to deeds.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q04/p1", "position": "God raises the physically dead for resurrection and recompense.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Yahya, Ibn Abbas and others give resurrection; al-Qurtubi prefers it as a reply to unbelievers; Abu Hayyan rejects the faith metaphor as remote. Al-Biqaʿi also sees gradual worldly revival before the collective Hour."}, {"id": "36:12/q04/p2", "position": "God brings people from disbelief or ignorance to faith.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan give this figurative reading; al-Kashshaf says from idolatry to faith; al-Biqaʿi allows spiritual rescue from obscurity. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi find it remote."}, {"id": "36:12/q04/p3", "position": "God revives dead hearts and inner faculties through faith, truth, service, disclosure, and witnessing.", "reasons": "Muhammad b. Ali al-Tirmidhi distinguishes souls, hearts, secrets, and inmost hearts; Study Quran reports the knowledge and truth interpretation."}, {"id": "36:12/q04/p4", "position": "God revives the dead earth.", "reasons": "Study Quran attributes this reading to IK and cites 57:17."}, {"id": "36:12/q04/p5", "position": "It refers to deeds.", "reasons": "Jishumi transmits this unusual gloss from Mujahid without further explanation."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q05", "question": "Why is نحيي inflected as it is?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q05/p1", "position": "Its ḍamma is omitted for heaviness, and the two yāʾs cannot assimilate because that would juxtapose two vowelless letters.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas gives both morphological constraints."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q06", "question": "Why does resurrection appear before recording?", "turns_on": "Whether the order reflects the aim of recording or the grandeur of resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q06/p1", "position": "Resurrection is the purpose that makes the record consequential.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says writing comes first in time, but without revival and reckoning it has no effect; al-Alusi says the effect of angelic writing appears then."}, {"id": "36:12/q06/p2", "position": "Resurrection is the greater divine act, so its prominence magnifies it.", "reasons": "Al-Razi connects the order to the majestic emphasis."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q07", "question": "What does God's writing of deeds signify?", "turns_on": "Whether writing is an actual deed register, a figure for recompense or knowledge, or paired with prior inscription.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q07/p1", "position": "Deeds and traces are entered in angelic or individual deed records.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says angelic writing is ascribed to God by His command; Tabatabai distinguishes personal books from the universal Imam; Elmalılı says pre-event Tablet inscription is followed by writing after action."}, {"id": "36:12/q07/p2", "position": "Writing stands for recompense.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan gives recompense alongside comprehensive knowledge; al-Alusi prefers the metonym because writing follows resurrection in the wording."}, {"id": "36:12/q07/p3", "position": "Writing means preserving deeds in God's knowledge.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan connects the metaphor to exhaustive knowledge fixed by writing; al-Alusi transmits a view that God neither forgets nor neglects acts."}, {"id": "36:12/q07/p4", "position": "Writing shows a prior record of what people will do, then a record as they do it.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports the predetermination explanation; Elmalılı says things are known and written beforehand and recorded afterward for accountability."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q08", "question": "How is ما قدموا construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q08/p1", "position": "It is the object of the active نكتب, with آثارهم coordinated with it.", "reasons": "Al-Samin describes the common active reading; al-Nahhas says a genitive complement stands in place of an omitted governing noun."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q09", "question": "What have people sent ahead?", "turns_on": "Whether قدموا denotes all acts, only good acts, intentions, or an implied pair including later effects.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q09/p1", "position": "Their deeds performed in worldly life, good and evil.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and others give the general deed gloss. Al-Biqaʿi includes acts, states and words, recorded with ensoulment; Study Quran says these testify for or against people. Al-Razi calls them deeds brought into existence; Islahi includes afterlife-directed and worldly acts."}, {"id": "36:12/q09/p2", "position": "Their good works, contrasted with misguidance left behind.", "reasons": "Mujahid is reported this way by Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Wahidi, al-Durr and Ibn Kathir."}, {"id": "36:12/q09/p3", "position": "Their intentions, preceding the resulting deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports the possibility; Tabatabai finds it contextually remote; al-Alusi says angels cannot see or record intentions."}, {"id": "36:12/q09/p4", "position": "Both what they did earlier and what they left for later.", "reasons": "Al-Razi sees one side of the pair as implying the other, comparing 16:81's clothing protecting from heat while also protecting from cold."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q10", "question": "How do deeds and traces relate?", "turns_on": "Whether the pair contrasts acts with enduring effects or intentions with acts.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q10/p1", "position": "Direct acts are distinguished from effects that endure or are followed afterward.", "reasons": "Abu Ali and al-Jubbaʾi contrast acts without and with continuing effects; Ibn Atiyya says the categories overlap but naming both stresses enduring remembrance; Islahi includes acts done for later generations."}, {"id": "36:12/q10/p2", "position": "Intentions are sent ahead and actual deeds are their traces.", "reasons": "Al-Razi gives this alternative; Tabatabai rejects it as far from context, and al-Alusi notes reports that angels cannot record hidden intentions."}]}
